Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda. This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations (UN), and the second largest in history. The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak. Testing and treatment are under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added. The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is not yet any treatment or vaccine for this strain. DR Congo's previous deadliest outbreak saw 2,299 deaths recorded between 2018-2020, the UN said. full_text: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly home Ruchira Ranasingha, 50, has been stranded in the Cook Islands since 2023 and wants to return to Sri Lanka. When Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific. The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged". Ranasingha had been hoping to settle in New Zealand. After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa. Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka. Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed. Lake Powell, the second-largest human-made reservoir in the US, has lost nearly 7% of its potential storage capacity since 1963, when Glen Canyon Dam was built, a new report shows. In addition to water loss due to anintense multiyear drought, the US Geological Survey and the Bureau of Reclamationreport found, Lake Powell faced an average annual loss in storage capacity of about 33,270 acre-feet, or 11 billion gallons, per year between 1963 and 2018. That’s enough water to fill the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall about 1,600 times. The capacity of the reservoir is shrinking because of sediments flowing in from theColorado and San Juan rivers, according to the report. Those sediments settle at the bottom of the reservoir and decrease the total amount of water the reservoir can hold. As of Monday, Lake Powell was around 25% full, according to data from the Bureau of Reclamation. It’s bad news for a region already facing water shortages and extreme wildfires due to the drought. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration drought experts said last week these conditions areexpected to at least continue– if not worsen – in the coming months. Lake Powell is an important reservoir in the Colorado River Basin. Both Lake Powell and nearby Lake Mead, the nation’s largest reservoir, have drained at an alarming rate. full_text: Judge dismisses Trump's $20 billion defamation lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letter A federal judge dismisses Trump's $20 billion Wall Street Journal lawsuit over its Epstein birthday letter report. A US federal judge has dismissed PresidentDonald Trump's $20 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal for the second time. The case concerned the newspaper's report about a sexually suggestive birthday letter allegedly bearing Trump's name and addressed to convicted sex offenderJeffrey Epstein. US District Judge Darrin P. Gayles ruled on Saturday, October 31, that Trump had not shown enough evidence to establish that the newspaper acted with actual malice when it published the report. The latest decision also means Trump cannot file another amended complaint in the same case. Trump argued that The Wall Street Journal should not have published the report after he denied writing the letter. However, Gayles rejected that claim, saying a public figure's denial does not prevent journalists from reporting on an allegation. “Were that the law, any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press,” the judge wrote. In defamation cases involving public figures, plaintiffs must show that a publication acted with actual malice. This means they must establish that the publisher knew the statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for whether it was true. Gayles found that Trump's revised complaint still failed to meet this requirement.
